Taking Homes, Giving Homes: Property Seizure and Redistribution in Occupied Mariupol

TOT Insights and the Centre for the Study of Occupation. July 2026.
Key findings
  • Homes whose owners are absent or have not re-registered under Russian rule are reclassified as ownerless and transferred to a municipal fund, so that keeping a home now turns on physical presence, Russian documentation and political compliance rather than prior title.
  • The compensation queue held 5,822 households as of late May, the first distribution covered 1,890 apartments, and at least 3,932 remained waiting, so seized property is being used to fill the gap.
  • Around 800 apartments, roughly seventeen per cent of the declared compensation fund of 4,778, are reserved as a service fund for imported Russian officials, security staff and specialists.

In occupied Mariupol, the destruction of housing has become an opportunity to remake who owns the city. Through a procedure that reclassifies the homes of absent owners as ownerless and feeds them into a municipal fund, the occupation administration rehouses selected residents and imported Russian personnel out of property taken from those who fled or who refuse the Russian system. The June 2026 monitoring shows this has moved from occasional cases to a continuous mass programme, and that the decisive factor in whether a person keeps their home has become presence, documents and loyalty rather than prior ownership.

How a home becomes “ownerless”

The core mechanism is an administrative pipeline that converts absence into loss of title. An apartment is added to a district list where the owner is not present, lacks a Russian passport, has not completed document re-registration or has not received notification, after which an inspection is carried out and the property can pass into municipal ownership and be reused. This matters because the burden is inverted: it is the owner who must prove the validity of their right inside a system built by the occupying power, so a person who has fled the war or cannot travel is structurally disadvantaged from the outset.

The process now runs as a permanent cycle rather than a one-off campaign, and it reaches across the whole city. New listings appear continuously while previously listed apartments move to the next stage of registration, and the procedure covers all four districts, concentrated where destruction, dismantling and new construction coincide, including the central Zhovtnevyi district where land values and commercial attractiveness are highest. This matters because it indicates scale and continuity: the administration has established a standing procedure for reclassifying title, weighted towards the locations where the reclaimed property is most valuable.

Housing some residents at the expense of others

A central feature of the policy is that the housing handed to one resident is often taken from another. A person who lost an apartment in a demolished building may be rehoused in a new-build or in an apartment whose owner's right was terminated for absence, so the administration is replacing the pre-war ownership structure with a new one, in which the right to housing is set by a Russian commission's decision rather than by prior title. This matters because it turns reconstruction into redistribution, allowing the authorities to demonstrate a social result while the source of the housing stock stays hidden.

That concealment is built into how the policy is communicated. Public notices emphasise the number of apartments issued, but whether a given apartment is newly built, a service flat or property seized from another owner is generally not disclosed, so the resident sees only the final stage, the handover of keys. This matters because it deprives both the new occupant and the dispossessed owner of the truth about the transaction, and it lets a programme of property transfer present itself as an act of provision.

Who keeps a home, and who loses one

The procedure creates two classes of Mariupol resident with opposite outcomes. Those who are in the city, hold Russian documents and can deal with the Rosreestr registration system in person are able to preserve or formalise their right, while those who are outside the occupied territory, cannot return or will not recognise the Russian system find that their absence becomes the grounds for losing their property. This matters because ownership now depends on physical presence, political loyalty and a willingness to use Russian state services, which converts a question of legal title into a test of compliance.

The Rosreestr cadastral assessment then makes the transfer permanent and profitable. Once boundaries are set and a cadastral value assigned, a property acquires a figure for taxation, sale, lease, withdrawal and development, and an apartment or plot whose owner has not confirmed their right can be moved into the municipal fund and folded into a new investment or construction project. This matters because it closes the loop: the same system that removes an absent owner's title also prepares that home to be sold or redeveloped, with the whole property and land portfolio controlled by a small federally connected management team under the administration head Anton Koltsov.

Rebuilding, and for whom

Alongside rehousing residents, the administration is reserving a substantial share of the stock for imported Russians. A separate service fund of around 800 apartments across six buildings, about seventeen per cent of the declared compensation fund of 4,778 apartments, is being used to settle officials, court and prosecution staff, FSB and Rosgvardia personnel, doctors, teachers, builders and engineers through official housing, subsidised rent and mortgage programmes. This matters because it shows the policy serves the occupation's own personnel as well as the people of Mariupol.

Taken together, housing has become a demographic instrument. It rewards residents who return and register so as not to lose their place, secures imported Russian workers, and reshapes the internal map of the city as people are rehoused in districts other than their own, dissolving pre-war communities in the process. This matters because the redistribution is doing long-term political work, remaking who lives where and who belongs, so that even where a building is genuinely repaired the outcome is a reordered population rather than a restored one.

Conclusion

Housing in Mariupol has become an instrument of governance. By deciding who may keep a home, who receives one and whose is taken, the administration rewards presence and loyalty, dispossesses the absent, and reserves a share for its own imported staff, and the scale reached in June shows this is now a systematic programme rather than a set of isolated cases. The people most exposed are those who left to escape the war or who refuse Russian documents, for whom absence is being converted into permanent loss.

Field evidence

Sources and method

This briefing synthesises monitoring of occupied Mariupol by the Centre for the Study of Occupation (CSO), June 2026, which draws in turn on Russian federal, regional and occupation sources. The underlying June 2026 monitoring is held in the hub's private repository under its closed-monitoring and restricted-data policy, and is not published alongside this briefing. The queue, distribution and service-fund figures, and the district detail, originate in those occupation sources and are presented as their claims rather than as independently verified fact, consistent with CSO methodology.

Primary sources flagged in the CSO monitoring (occupation outlet MRPL.NEWS):

  • Nationalisation of the apartments of a further 25 Mariupol residents
  • Rosreestr strategic session on preparation for cadastral assessment
  • Determination of land-plot boundaries, key steps and requirements
